talks.title: Keynote
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Keynote.
talks.summary:
Overview: A US Cyber Command executive director delivers the CyberWarCon keynote on China's cyber threat to national security and Cyber Command's elevation from tactical to strategic operations.

Key Topics: PRC cyber threats to national security; Cyber Command's global cyberspace operations coordination; adversary economies of scale targeting backbone infrastructure; and named intrusion sets including Flax Typhoon and Volt Typhoon.

Technical Details: The speaker describes adversary focus on valid credential abuse and privileged account targeting at scale, identifying numerous PRC-associated intrusion sets targeting critical infrastructure and defense industrial base.

Takeaways: Nation-state adversaries achieve economies of scale in cyberspace targeting shared infrastructure. Defenders must prioritize credential security and backbone infrastructure protection against PRC operations.

talks.title: The Nearest Neighbor Attack: How A Russian APT Weaponized Nearby Wi-Fi Networks for Covert Access
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The Nearest Neighbor Attack: How A Russian APT Weaponized Nearby Wi-Fi Networks for Covert Access.
talks.summary:
Talk Premise

Volexity president Stephen Adair introduces the "nearest neighbor attack," describing Russian APT use of nearby Wi-Fi for covert access based on a challenging 2022 engagement the firm can now discuss publicly.

Initial Detection

Investigation began with a custom Carbon Black Defend query flagging ser task.bat in ProgramData launching reg.exe to dump SYSTEM, SECURITY, and SAM hives into out.zip—typical credential-theft behavior on a server.

Early Timeline Clues

EDR showed an unprivileged organizational user RDP'd to the box, extracted defragment serve.zip with WinRAR GUI, and executed bundled scripts. A suspicious unsigned WaysGoose52.dll appeared under a fake Adobe directory with Print Spooler as parent process.

Forensics Response

Volexity prioritizes live memory acquisition over full disk imaging, pushing their Surge collector over RPC while continuing analysis. Adair frames the story as combining zero-day exploitation, skilled tradecraft, and innovative proximity-based access, with geopolitical espionage motivations.

talks.title: Adversarial Targeting of Critical Infrastructure Linchpins
talks.teaser: Intent explores Adversarial Targeting of Critical Infrastructure Linchpins.
talks.summary:
Three adversary tiers

Kyle Cas and colleagues profile OT/ICS threat actors at rising sophistication: Army of Russia Reborn (CAR), Cyber Avengers, and Volt Typhoon (Vanguard Panda). They use a sports analogy from freshman to varsity skill levels.

Disruption-focused groups

CAR, linked to Russian activists and poor OPSEC, brute-forces exposed VNC/HMI systems, publishes playbooks, and has caused real facility flooding and pressure manipulation. Cyber Avengers—a small IRGC-affiliated team—targets Israeli OT vendors like Unitronics, compromising perimeter devices and developing Linux ICS-oriented malware.

Strategic espionage

Volt Typhoon differs by sustained collection of OT project data, work logs, alerts, safety systems, and remediation procedures—intelligence to craft disruptive capabilities, not mere espionage. They live off the land with NPS tunnels, Impacket, web shells, and Soho router botnets, targeting interdependent fuel, water, and power providers serving military customers—the linchpins of critical infrastructure.

talks.title: RT's Covert Information Operations
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning RT's Covert Information Operations.
talks.summary:
## RT's Strategic Problem

Google Threat Analysis Group researcher Zach Butler explains how Russian state media outlet RT reaches global audiences in multiple languages but has been banned or restricted in many countries since 2014, most sharply after 2022. Losing platforms means losing reach.

## Covert Re-entry Tactics

RT responds by operating through brands that hide their affiliation. When a channel is discovered and removed, they spin up new ones. Butler documents three content strategies: original documentaries, reposted RT material with watermarks removed, and co-opted ideologically aligned influencers.

## Examples and Style

Covert brands like Dig Deep Documentary produce English-language, high-production content in classic RT style—sometimes literally repackaged RT videos. Influencer repost channels mirror talking-head commentary aligned with RT messaging goals without creator consent.

## Broader Implications

Butler notes similar tactics appear beyond RT, suggesting a shared playbook for evading platform bans. The talk highlights how state propaganda adapts to moderation by laundering identity through seemingly independent media brands.
